title: In hazy Asia, contrition helps clear the air
text:
In hazy Asia, contrition helps clear the air
Indonesia’s apology for clouds of smoke wafting over its neighbors might have aided new cooperation in Southeast Asia on preventing forest fires.
Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, offered an apology this week to the neighboring nations of Malaysia and Singapore for the record land fires – totaling about the size of Delaware – that have polluted the skies in much of Southeast Asia this year.
His official contrition for the toxic haze included a measure of repentance and reform.
Mr. Prabowo said his government was “forced to take very tough measures” against the main culprits for the fires – companies burning forests and peatlands to clear land for palm oil and pulpwood plantations. Indonesia also has had a severe dry season, making it difficult to contain the fires.
He said 26 companies are under investigation, 11 others have been charged, and 17 have had their permits revoked. The Philippines’ foreign minister said she appreciated the “very frank and candid” remarks by the Indonesian leader about the efforts to control the fires, most of which are on the islands of Borneo, Sumatra, and Papua.
If Mr. Prabowo was seeking a pardon for lax enforcement of regulations for slash-and-burn agricultural practices, it might have come in the mercy extended by the other 10 member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). At a summit in Manila, Philippines, last weekend, the leaders worked together on tightening up their agreements on addressing transboundary haze pollution.
In any part of the world where environmental hazards cross a border, anger and threats are often the first reactions. A Malaysian official, for example, has called Indonesia an “outcast” within ASEAN. Singapore has moved toward taking legal action against Indonesian companies suspected of starting the fires.
Yet sometimes, meekness and then reform can open the hearts of neighbors to forgive and work together on solutions, as well as restore the bonds of neighborly affection.
In his remarks, Mr. Prabowo echoed this idea. He said that “close cooperation, honesty between neighbors, [and] the fact that we have to work together in full transparency will strengthen us.”
After the ASEAN summit, the body’s secretary-general noted a shift in tone during the negotiations. Kao Kim Hourn told the network CNA that this is the “first time that I heard this issue being discussed quite sensibly by the leaders.” The apology by Indonesia might have been just the grease to renew their partnership.
